idiom_name: Forwardable#def_delegators, or Delegator/SimpleDelegator from the standard library
implementation_notes: Ruby ships the pattern in its standard library: `Forwardable` generates forwarding methods for the members you name (`def_delegators :@records, :size, :<<, :map`), which is what you want over a known, narrow API, while `SimpleDelegator` forwards every supported method call to the object passed to its constructor and can switch the delegate later with `__setobj__`. Both replace the hand-written forwarders plain Ruby (`def size = @records.size`) would need; `method_missing` plus `respond_to_missing?` is the third, dynamic form when the forwarded names cannot be listed. Prefer Forwardable when the surface is deliberate and SimpleDelegator when the whole object must be wrapped.
code_sketch:
require 'forwardable'

class CountingStore
  extend Forwardable
  def_delegators :@inner, :load, :size         # generated forwarding methods

  def initialize(inner) = (@inner = inner)
  def save(id) = (@count = (@count || 0) + 1; @inner.save(id))   # override one member
end
pitfalls: `def_delegators` defines methods at class-definition time: a name the delegate does not support raises NoMethodError inside the delegate, and new delegate APIs are not picked up - for open-ended forwarding use SimpleDelegator or method_missing.

`method_missing`-based delegation must also define `respond_to_missing?` (and use `public_send` for private members), otherwise `respond_to?`, duck-type checks and library introspection give wrong answers.

`SimpleDelegator#__setobj__` changes the delegate without changing the wrapper's method set, so swapping to an object of a different type produces surprising behaviour; identity (`equal?`, `hash`) stays with the wrapper, not the delegate.
